one_line.text: American psychologist (1908–1970) who founded humanistic psychology's 'third force', proposed the hierarchy of needs, and spent his last years mapping self-actualization and transcendence.

biography.text: Born in Brooklyn to Jewish immigrant parents, Maslow trained in experimental psychology, taught at Brooklyn College and then Brandeis University, and served as president of the American Psychological Association in 1968. Against the era's dominant behaviourism and psychoanalysis he built a 'third force' studying healthy, growing people rather than pathology: the hierarchy of needs (1943), Motivation and Personality (1954), and Toward a Psychology of Being (1962). He died of a heart attack in June 1970; The Farther Reaches of Human Nature was assembled from his late essays and lectures by his wife Bertha Maslow with Henry Geiger.

background.text: His method was deliberately unorthodox: instead of averaging across subjects, he studied the exceptional — people he judged self-actualized, from historical figures to acquaintances — to ask what humans are like at their best. That choice made his psychology generative and quotable, and left it resting on samples no modern review board would recognise.

expertise.text: A credentialed academic psychologist and APA president whose authority in his own field was institutional as well as intellectual; his late-life claims about transcendence and values, however, deliberately stepped past what his evidence could carry, and he said as much, framing them as a programme for future science.

perspective_and_limits.text: Maslow writes as psychology's great optimist: a scientist convinced that human nature's upper range is real data. The perspective produced a vocabulary — self-actualization, peak experiences — that entered the language, and limits that critics have pressed ever since: loose sampling, definitions that drift, cultural narrowness in what counts as the highest human life, and an empirical record for the hierarchy that later research left largely unsupported.
